messages.subject_clean: Request for advice on interpretation of results on lavaan by applying the CFA
messages.body_plain:
These results and the syntax don't match. In particular, your results include:

Regressions:

                   Estimate  Std.Err  z-value  P(>|z|)

  QUAL ~

    SAT               0.688    0.180    3.828    0.000

  SAT ~

    FID               0.224       NA

Covariances:

                   Estimate  Std.Err  z-value  P(>|z|)

 .QUAL ~~

   .SAT              -0.215    0.078   -2.752    0.006

 .SAT ~~

    FID               0.135       NA

Your syntax says nothing about residual covariances between Qual and Sat and between Sat and Fid. Also, your degrees of freedom do not match my expectations for your syntax.

     It is pointless to evaluate fit until you are estimating the correct model. However, it would be naive to expect a model with 19 indicators for one factor to fit well, and all fit information here points to a poor fit, with the evidence muted by your low sample size of 100.

messages.subject: higher order
messages.body_plain:
Hello!

I wanted to know more about output of the higher order using the summary() and inspect().
If I were create a normal CFA, the latent covariance matrix is below. The summary() and inspect() are identical results.

Covariances:
                        Estimate  Std.Err  z-value  P(>|z|)   Std.lv  Std.all
  Factor1 ~~
    Factor2           0.423    0.070    6.028    0.000    0.813    0.813
  Factor2 ~~
    Factor3           0.232    0.045    5.148    0.000    0.785    0.785
  Factor1 ~~
    Factor3           0.349    0.049    7.072    0.000    0.692    0.692

> inspect(fit.first, what='cov.lv <http://cov.lv>')
            Factr1 Factr2 Factr3
Factor1 0.885
Factor2 0.423  0.306
Factor3 0.349  0.232  0.287

This looks great, and I create a higher order factor model.
It looks fine from the output.

 Higher order =~
    Factor1           1.000                                 0.732    0.732
    Factor2           0.732       NA                      0.912    0.912
    Factor3           0.728       NA                      0.936    0.936

But when I look at the output of the model using the summary().
This isn't what I expect.

Covariances:
                         Estimate  Std.Err  z-value  P(>|z|)   Std.lv  Std.all
Factor1 ~~
    Factor2           0.076    0.066    1.141    0.254    0.519    0.519
  Factor2 ~~
    Factor3          -0.020    0.020   -1.043    0.297   -0.476   -0.476
  Factor1 ~~
    Factor3           0.003    0.051    0.066    0.947    0.028    0.028

And oddly enough, if I use inspect(), the result is the same as the CFA model instead of the higher order CFA.

> inspect(fit, what='cor.lv <http://cor.lv>')
             Factr1 Factr2 Factr3 Parano
Factor1  1.000
Factor2  0.813  1.000
Factor3  0.692  0.785  1.000
Paranoia 0.732  0.912  0.936  1.000

> inspect(fit, what='cov.lv <http://cov.lv>')
             Factr1 Factr2 Factr3 Parano
Factor1  0.885
Factor2  0.423  0.306
Factor3  0.349  0.232  0.287
Paranoia 0.475  0.348  0.345  0.475

So my question is why is the output from the summary() that shows the latent covariance different from the inspect()?
And also, why is the covariance estimates of the covariance so bad when I use a higher order cfa?

Thank you!
Aiden

messages.subject: Re: higher order
messages.body_plain:
Aidan--
     All is not well. The "covariances" you see in the higehr order model are residual covariances, not total covariances. As free parameters, they make your higher order model not identified, which is why you have "NA"s for the standard errors of the loadings of the first order factors on the second order factor. The correation matrix you get from Inspect shows the toal correlations, not the residual correlations.
     You should fix the covariances among first order factors to 0 and re-estimate the model. When you do, you will find that its chi-square fit is identical to the fit of the model without the higher order factor.

messages.subject_clean: Convergence problem only with robust estimators
messages.body_plain:
Hello, I'm new to lavaan and would appreciate your help with a convergence problem I'm having.

I'm running a random-intercept cross-lagged panel model, with 3 variables cross-lagged over 3 waves of data (n=1704, df=4).

Using the default (fiml) for missing values, and ML as the estimator, the model converges with good fit and expected estimates.

I want, however, to try out robust estimators (due to skew in the data). When I select MLM (complete data only) or even MLF or MLR (which should deal with the missingness in my data), the model doesn't converge.

Any ideas as to why this might be, or what I can do to fix it?

I can post the model syntax and/or more information if it helps.

Cheers,

Russell

Cheers,
Vaib

messages.subject: Re: higher order
messages.body_plain:
Aidan--
     This is factor-based SEM 101. The factor model implies a covariance matrix for the observed variables, where each element of that matrix is a function of model parameters. Estimating those parameters means, in effect, solving for them out of that model-implied covariance matrix, using the elements of the sample-based covariance matrix as "knowns" to assign values to the "unknowns," the free model parameters. You can only solve for a certain parameter out of certain elements of the model-implied covariance matrix, because each parameter only appears in the formula for certain elements. You effectively consume elements once you use them to solve for one parameter--you can't use the same information over and over again to solve for parameter after parameter.
     With a higehr order factor model, you must think a little differently. Now you are solving out of the covariance matrix of the factors. The parameters for the higher order factor model--both the loadings of firt order factor and second order factor,m and the residual variances and covariances of the first order factors--are solved out of the covariance matrix of the factors. With three factors, there are only 3 ( 3-1) / 2 = 6 elements of the factor covariance matrix. That is the most parameters that you can estimate. With NO free residual covariances among the factors, you consume all 6 elements of this matrix. As soon as you try to estimate one residual covariance, your model is not identified. A model with three freely covarying factors involves the same number of free parameters--that is why this higehr order model and the freely covarying factor model are equivalent.

messages.body_plain:
Edward,

Okay. With higher order models you are effectively calculating DFs separately for the observed covariance matrix and the factor covariance matrix. So in instances like this, a higher order model with only two latent factors and one higher order factor should not work because you have 2(2+1)/2 = 3 known parameters, but you need to estimate 2 factor loadings, and 2 factor residuals, which would result in a negative df (3-4 = -1). Unless you fix to factor residuals or to factor loadings to zero, which would than just be a regular CFA.

With NO free residual covariances among the factors, you consume all 6 elements of this matrix. As soon as you try to estimate one residual covariance, your model is not identified. A model with three freely covarying factors involves the same number of free parameters--that is why this higehr order model and the freely covarying factor model are equivalent.

As free parameters, they make your higher order model not identified, which is why you have "NA"s for the standard errors of the loadings of the first order factors on the second order factor. messages.subject: Re: BIC ML versus MLR
messages.body_plain:
> Shouldn't it be the case that the information indices in the ML column when estimating using estimator='mlr' should reflect the estimator='ml' BIC, rather than be identical to the MLR BIC? And if not, could you suggest why not?

The robust correction is made to the test statistic to make it more approximately chi-squared distributed.  Information criteria are not test statistics, so they have no associated Type I error rate to correct (unless you define errors in model ranking, rather than in reference to a theoretical distribution of the statistic).  In lavaan, Mplus, and most other packages I am familiar with, information criteria are calculated from the likelihood of the data given the model parameters (which are not corrected by robust procedures because they are still consistent even if continuous data are not normal)

> -2*LL0 + log(N)k

where LL0 is the log-likelihood of the data under the fitted model's parameters.

> fitMeasures(fitmlR, c("ntotal","npar","logl","bic"))
   ntotal      npar      logl       bic
  301.000    30.000 -3737.745  7646.703

> -2*fitMeasures(fitmlR, "logl") + log(fitMeasures(fitmlR, "ntotal"))*fitMeasures(fitmlR, "npar")
7646.703

Some packages (and textbooks) do calculate BIC as ChiSq + log(N)k instead of -2*LL0 + log(N)k, where ChiSq is -2 times the difference between LL1 (log-likelihood under the saturated model) and LL0.  Because all competing models use the same LL1 when calculating their ChiSq, the model rankings are equivalent using either formula.  This, I suppose, is why you expect there would be a robust version of information criteria, but the robust correction applied to ChiSq has nothing to do with how information criteria are used.

It is still correct to recognize that the (log-)likelihood of the data is incorrect when data are not normal, because we are calculating the likelihood assuming data are multivariate normally distributed; thus, information criteria based on normal-likelihoods are not valid.  A correct likelihood would require knowing what the true distribution is, as well as how to link estimated model parameters to the parameters of that distribution so we can calculate valid (log-)likelihoods.  However, a robust correction is not meant to make our assumptions valid.  Rather, it is meant to return valid tests in spite of our assumptions being invalid.  For example, our application of robust SEs to calculate robust Wald z statistics still assumes a normal sampling distribution of the sample statistics (that's where we get our p values).  But it is not necessarily the case that the statistics are normally distributed when our data are not MVN distributed (the true sampling distribution might be skewed, varying more in one direction than in another). messages.subject: Re: What is the difference between srmr and srmr_bollen fit measures?
messages.subject_clean: What is the difference between srmr and srmr_bollen fit measures?
messages.body_plain:
> what is the difference between srmr and srmr_bollen fit measures reported by lava an package?

The default SRMR is calculated using Bollen's formula (found in his 1989 book), which first standardized both the observed and model-implied covariance matrices, then subtracts them to calculate standardized residuals (differences between observed and expected correlations).  So in lavaan's fitMeasures(), you will always see the same value for srmr and srmr_bollen.

resid(fit, type = "cor")
resid(fit, type = "cor.bollen")

SRMR can also be caculated using Bentler's formula (found in his EQS manual), which first calculates unstandardized covariance residuals, then standardized them using the model-implied variances. Sort of arbitrary, and often makes little to no difference in practice unless constraints are put on residual variances, so that the model-implied variances are not identical to observed variances.

resid(fit, type = "cor.bentler")

I like Bentler's formula because it includes information about misspecification regarding variance estimates.  Bollen's formula will always return zeros on the diagonal because it subtracts 2 correlation matrices, so it is a bit less informative.  However, Bentler's method standardizes differences relative to model-implied variances only, whereas Bollen's method standardizes each matrix relative to its own diagonal elements.  Again, it's probably of little consequence in practice, but Mplus uses Bentler's formula for diagonal elements and Bollen's formula for off-diagonal elements (srmr_mplus).

Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

messages.body_plain:
> but this is not the effect that I am looking for (?) (i.e. whether there is an overall difference in slope), since I am interested in the difference of the slope between groups.

What about the slope?  The average slope?  The syntax that constraints the slope (co)variances to zero posits that individuals (within both groups) have identical trajectories.  If you want to compare the average slope across groups, you need to constrain that parameter to equality

s ~ c(a1, a1)*1

> 1. Is there a way of constraining the slopes per group with the growth() function?
> (do I use 'group =' or not?)

If you want to compare groups, you need the group= argument.  Are you asking about the group.equal= argument?  Specifying group.equal = "means" would constrain all latent means to equality across groups, which is not what you want.  Use the syntax I showed above.

> 3. Is this approach also applicable when investigating the full model including the predictors?

If you have predictors of the slope, then you are comparing intercepts across groups.  Thus, the test would be conditional on how your predictors are centered.  This is the same as the homogeneity of slopes assumption when comparing "adjusted means" in ANCOVA (equivalent to comparing intercepts).  To make an unconditional test of equality of intercepts, the effects of predictors on the latent growth factors would have to be constrained to equality across groups.  You should test that set of constraints first, to make sure it holds.  If it does not, then that implies an interaction between the predictor(s) and the Randomization variable.  In which case you could probe the interaction by centering the predictors at 2 or 3 meaningful values, and testing equivalence of intercepts at each of those values.

http://quantpsy.org/interact/lca2.htm

messages.body_plain:
> Is it possible in Lavaan to check for more than three groups. How does lavaan account for multiple comparisons if at all

The same methods apply to an arbitrary number of groups.  The tests are omnibus, so when you constrain loadings, intercepts, etc. across groups, you do so across all groups, and the change in model fit tells you whether that set of constraints is tenable.  If not, you could perform pairwise follow-up tests constraining parameters across pairs of groups at a time, but I'm not sure that is advisable (haven't seen any literature demonstrating its utility).  You could ask on SEMNET, since this isn't a lavaan issue but a general SEM issue:

On Monday, 9 October 2017 08:54:41 UTC+1, Terrence Jorgensen wrote:
> > Shouldn't it be the case that the information indices in the ML column when estimating using estimator='mlr' should reflect the estimator='ml' BIC, rather than be identical to the MLR BIC? And if not, could you suggest why not?
>
> The robust correction is made to the test statistic to make it more approximately chi-squared distributed.  Information criteria are not test statistics, so they have no associated Type I error rate to correct (unless you define errors in model ranking, rather than in reference to a theoretical distribution of the statistic).  In lavaan, Mplus, and most other packages I am familiar with, information criteria are calculated from the likelihood of the data given the model parameters (which are not corrected by robust procedures because they are still consistent even if continuous data are not normal)
>
> > -2*LL0 + log(N)k
>
> where LL0 is the log-likelihood of the data under the fitted model's parameters.
>
> > fitMeasures(fitmlR, c("ntotal","npar","logl","bic"))
>    ntotal      npar      logl       bic
>   301.000    30.000 -3737.745  7646.703
>
> > -2*fitMeasures(fitmlR, "logl") + log(fitMeasures(fitmlR, "ntotal"))*fitMeasures(fitmlR, "npar")
> 7646.703
>
> Some packages (and textbooks) do calculate BIC as ChiSq + log(N)k instead of -2*LL0 + log(N)k, where ChiSq is -2 times the difference between LL1 (log-likelihood under the saturated model) and LL0.  Because all competing models use the same LL1 when calculating their ChiSq, the model rankings are equivalent using either formula.  This, I suppose, is why you expect there would be a robust version of information criteria, but the robust correction applied to ChiSq has nothing to do with how information criteria are used.
>
> It is still correct to recognize that the (log-)likelihood of the data is incorrect when data are not normal, because we are calculating the likelihood assuming data are multivariate normally distributed; thus, information criteria based on normal-likelihoods are not valid.  A correct likelihood would require knowing what the true distribution is, as well as how to link estimated model parameters to the parameters of that distribution so we can calculate valid (log-)likelihoods.  However, a robust correction is not meant to make our assumptions valid.  Rather, it is meant to return valid tests in spite of our assumptions being invalid.  For example, our application of robust SEs to calculate robust Wald z statistics still assumes a normal sampling distribution of the sample statistics (that's where we get our p values).  But it is not necessarily the case that the statistics are normally distributed when our data are not MVN distributed (the true sampling distribution might be skewed, varying more in one direction than in another).  The robust correction just makes sure we don't have inflated Type I error rates when we infer whether parameters differ from zero in the population.
>

> Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
> Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
> UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.body_plain:
Dear Terrence and fellow lavaaners,

Sorry for bumping this discussion, but only now I could return to this problem.

indProb seems to be what I need to solve it, however I need further help on how to use it. For that, I will use a simpler model than the one originally posted. Please consider the model specification below:
model7 <- “
    sch =~ pos_2grp+ neg_2grp+ dis_2grp
    gen =~ BDNFord + EGFRord + IL3ord
    cog =~  attention + verbal + workingm

    sch ~ cprime * gen
    sch ~ b * cog
    sch ~ bprime * genXcog

    cog ~ a * gen
    cog ~~ genXcog
    gen ~~ genXcog

    bgen :=  b + bprime
    indgen := bgen * a
    indNgen := b * a
    indDiff := indgen - indNgen
 ”
fit7 <- sem(model7, dataset, estimator = "MLM")
summary(fit7)

Where sch is symptom severity measured in tests, cog is trivial cognitive testing (and the mediator) and gen is formed by ordinal variables (0=absence of risk allele, 1=heterozygous, 2=homozygous). The model I have in mind looks like the figure below, from the paper [^1]. On trying to run this specification, lavaan will complain that cog is not an observed variable and not run the analysis.

dataset<-indProd(dataset, var1=c("BDNFord","EGFRord","IL3ord"),

Thank you,

Luis

[^1]: Jeremy N.V Miles, Magdalena Kulesza, Brett Ewing, Regina A Shih, Joan S Tucker, Elizabeth J D’Amico, (2015) “Moderated
mediation analysis: an illustration using the association of gender with delinquency and mental health”, Journal of Criminal
Psychology, Vol. 5 Issue: 2, pp.99-123, https://doi.org/10.1108/JCP-02-2015-0010

> If you want to compare groups, you need the group= argument.  Are you asking about the group.equal= argument?  Specifying group.equal = "means" would constrain all latent means to equality across groups, which is not what you want.  Use the syntax I showed above.
>
> > 3. Is this approach also applicable when investigating the full model including the predictors?
>
> If you have predictors of the slope, then you are comparing intercepts across groups.  Thus, the test would be conditional on how your predictors are centered.  This is the same as the homogeneity of slopes assumption when comparing "adjusted means" in ANCOVA (equivalent to comparing intercepts).  To make an unconditional test of equality of intercepts, the effects of predictors on the latent growth factors would have to be constrained to equality across groups.  You should test that set of constraints first, to make sure it holds.  If it does not, then that implies an interaction between the predictor(s) and the Randomization variable.  In which case you could probe the interaction by centering the predictors at 2 or 3 meaningful values, and testing equivalence of intercepts at each of those values.
>
> http://quantpsy.org/interact/lca2.htm
>
> Terrence D. Jorgensen
> Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
> Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
> UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen
>

This is a general SEM question, not a lavaan question. You could try asking this question on semnet, a list devoted to structural equation modeling generally.
     You can find discussion of fit assessment in factor-based SEM in standard texts, like Rex Kline's. Using general criteria, this is not a good model for these data. Authorities would recommend that you screen out this model in favor of competing models. Modification indices would point you to areas where you could improve the fit of this model, on a purely data-driven, theory-free basis.

messages.body_plain:
The polychoric correlation only makes sense if data are ordinal. If data re continuous, there would be no good reason to discretize the data for purposes of computing a polychoric correlation matrix. Such an approach would sacrifice information.
     For information about lavaan in particular, the lavaan project is a very good source:
http://lavaan.ugent.be/resources/teaching.html

messages.subject: Re: Difference in DWLS estimator model fit in case of numeric and ordered data
messages.subject_clean: Difference in DWLS estimator model fit in case of numeric and ordered data
messages.body_plain:
Pawel,
Perhaps the source of the confusion here involves the scope of DWLS.  Today, DWLS is perhaps most commonly used in conjunction with threshold models for ordinal data.  However, it was developed independently and, I believe, earlier.  If I am not mistaken, DWLS was introduced into LISREL as a computationally less demanding alternative to WLS (ADF).  Both were presented as methods for modeling non-normal continuous data.  In this respect, DWLS differs from mean-adjusted and mean-and-variance-adjusted WLS which I believe were both developed specifically in the context of threshold models for categorical data.

So, when you choose DWLS in Lavaan, you are not automatically choosing to use threshold models.  You are simply choosing an estimation technique for the model that you specified.  You can confirm this by looking at the parameters listed in the summary output or parameter matrices. If you use DWLS to estimate a continuous variable model, you will not see thresholds among the parameters.

# The Holzinger and Swineford (1939) example
HS.model <- ' visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3
              textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
              speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9 '

fit <- lavaan(HS.model, data=HolzingerSwineford1939,
              auto.var=TRUE, auto.fix.first=TRUE,
              auto.cov.lv.x=TRUE, estimator='DWLS')

summary(fit)
lavInspect(object=fit, what='free')

Keith
------------------------
Keith A. Markus
John Jay College of Criminal Justice, CUNY
http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus
Frontiers of Test Validity Theory: Measurement, Causation and Meaning.
http://www.routledge.com/books/details/9781841692203/

messages.subject: Re: growth() model with two groups: equality constraints and 'group = '
messages.subject_clean: growth() model with two groups: equality constraints and 'group = '
messages.body_plain:
> would you suggest to use group.equal = c("regressions")? Or do it individually:

I would specify constraints explicitly in the model syntax, so you know exactly what you are doing.

> s ~ c(a1,a1)*Age+ c(a1,a1)*T0_educ + c(a1,a1)*Home_alone+ c(a1,a1)*Home_child+c(a1,a1)* T0_treatment_chemo_01+ c(a1,a1)*T0_revalidatie_01+
>    c(a1,a1)*T0_psych_01 + c(a1,a1)*T0_selfm_alg + c(a1,a1)*T0_selfm_coping + c(a1,a1)*T0_selfm_selfhelp
> '

This constrains all variables to have the same effect, which is not what you want to do.  You just want each variable's effect to be the same in both groups.

s ~ c(a1,a1)*Age+ c(b1,b1)*T0_educ + c(c1,c1)*Home_alone+ ...

> (can I also just use 's ~ c(a1, a1)*1' here?)

Again, don't use the same label to constrain intercepts across groups that you use to constrain other parameters across groups, because any parameter with the same label will be forced to have the same value.

But don't make this constraint yet.  First compare the unrestricted model (ModUN: no constraints across groups) to the model with constrained effects on the latent slope (ModHomog).

IFF (if and only if) that model comparison is not significant (refer to the anova() output), then compare ModHomog to a model with the same constraints but additionally constraints the intercepts across groups.  That second model-comparison will tell you whether the average slope significantly differs across groups, controlling for age, educ, etc.

> - individually -

>
> s ~ c(a1,a1)*Age+ T0_educ + Home_alone+ Home_child+ T0_treatment_chemo_01+ T0_revalidatie_01+
>    T0_psych_01 + T0_selfm_alg + T0_selfm_coping + T0_selfm_selfhelp
>

> With the latter I could test for each predictor whether there is an interaction with Randomization, which can be followed up with the steps you described.

Yes, that is correct.  But I would start with an omnibus test of whether all effects on the latent slope can be constrained across groups.  IFF that is significant, then at least one effect differs across groups, and you can conduct these individual tests as post-hoc comparisons to see which interactions need to be probed instead of making a single comparison of the intercept across groups, as described above.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.subject: Re: lavaan WARNING: some observed variances are (at least) a factor 1000 times larger than others
messages.subject_clean: lavaan WARNING: some observed variances are (at least) a factor 1000 times larger than others
messages.body_plain:
> what this practically means for my model. Does this mean I should not trust this particular model because these unequal variances make it unreliable?

The message is a warning because it might be a problem.  Estimators try to minimize the discrepancy between the observed and expected (i.e., model-implied) means and (co)variances.  If a variable has an observed variance == 1 and the model estimates imply it is only half as large, the discrepancy (residual) is only 1 - 0.5 = 0.5, but if a variable has an observed variance of 100, the same relative discrepancy (half as large: 50) is much larger in absolute magnitude (100-50=50).  So variables with much larger variances can dominate the estimation algorithm's search for the best-fitting parameter estimates, paying less attention to important discrepancies among variables with less variance.  Again, that is only a possibility, not a guarantee.

> Presumably, the variances are so large due to the values of the variables so should I transform my variables in some way?

Sure, you can divide the variable with large variance by 10 to express in larger units, so that the variance is 10^2 = 100 times smaller, making it closer in magnitude to other observed variances.  Assuming the estimator was not actually running into problems with the original data, you should get identical model fit, and your point and SE estimates involving the transformed variable should be the same except for a change in decimal place.

> Could it also be a result of some of my variables not being normally distributed?

No, nonnormal variables can also have either large or small variance.

> I am not actually using the errors and I am using the Wald test to investigate the fit of the model and the predictors so how concerned should I be about non-normality in my case?

Well, the Wald test for parameters also assumes normality of sampling distribution with the estimated SE, which assumes normal data.  Like with OLS regression, robustness to nonnormality is also a matter of degree, so it depends how must excess kurtosis the variables have.  To be conservative, you can use robust ML to adjust SEs and test statistics for nonnormality.  Some are available even with missing data when using FIML.

fit <- sem(model, data, missing = "FIML", estimator = "MLR")

messages.subject: Re: lavaan vs blavaan
messages.body_plain:
> I wonder what to make of a SEM model that as a non-significant P-value for Chi-square under DWLS but a significant P-value under Robust.

It's usually the other way around, since the robust correction is meant to correct for Type I error inflation (at least with continuous data, for which it was originally intended to be used).  But that is the average behavior over many samples.  You just have one sample, so you can't draw an inference about why this happened to happen.

The uncorrected test statistic is only provided for the sake of completion (and because it is used in the robust chi-squared difference test).  You should pay attention only to the robust column because that is the one expected to behave better on average across many samples.  However, you have a very small sample, and past research has shown that even this robust test statistic has inflated error rates until sample sizes are very large, especially when categories are asymmetric.

http://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/10705511.2014.859510

> I tried also the Bayesian version. But there, I do not get a test-statistic for too many missing data

Huh?  If you are looking for the chi-squared (derived from the minimum fit function using DWLS) in blavaan output, you won't find it with complete data because it is not a Bayesian statistic.  There is a PPP value, and some information criteria available for model comparison.

> Can I use the Bayesian parameter estimates and use the test-statistics from the frequentist analysis? Or is the data quality such that I should not use the SEM at all?

No, your test statistic is derived from the estimator, so you need to report one set of results or the other.  Again, you might be looking for something that isn't there in blavaan.  Perhaps this article will shed some light.

http://dx.doi.org/10.1037/a0026802

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.subject: Re: Cut edges not significant
messages.body_plain:
Ellias,
  This is not strictly a lavaan question and perhaps not even a SEM question given that you might accomplish your goals at least as well using OLS regression with lm(), unless your model is nonrecursive.

  The first thing that I notice is that your raw estimates equal your standardized estimates.  This suggests that you may be analyzing a correlation matrix.  Unless you include a compensatory set of nonlinear constraints in your model, analyzing a correlation matrix will generally give incorrect inferential statistics.  This happens because the variances on the diagonal are fixed to 1 but the inferential statistics assume that they are free to vary across samples.

  You are essentially engaged in an exercise of decomposing bivariate associations into conditional associations.  At one extreme, you could assume that every estimate exactly equals the population value.  This strategy has the advantage of giving you the optimal estimates of the population values and the disadvantage of giving you a conclusion unlikely to replicate on a new sample.  At the other extreme, you could adopt a rule that is insensitive to the data, such as concluding that all the regression weights are zero.  This would have the disadvantage of offering poor estimates of the population values, but would ensure guaranteed replication across samples.

  You are presumably looking for an intermediate approach that gives you a balance between these two extremes.  Adopting a fixed level of statistical significance offers one such intermediate approach.  It sounds as if you would like to nudge your approach closer to the second extreme, trading off accuracy of estimation for replicability by adopting a more simplified model.  This will mean greater model mispecification (due to simplification, two sides of the same coin).  One thing to consider is that if you apply the procedure iteratively, forcing one regression weight to zero can have an impact on other weights in the equation.

  By applying one rule in terms of the standardized regression weight to all pairs of variables, your approach essentially assumes that the scales of the variables provide no useful information relevant to your decision about keeping the regression weight.  I am not sure what you meant by 'experiment' but if you meant that you manipulated the independent variables, then their variances reflect the design rather than their natural variability.  So, a standardized conditional association involving an IV that has high natural variability may be more interesting than an equal standardized conditional association with an IV that has low natural variability.  So, adopting a fixed cut point for standardized regression weights may not offer the best strategy when used in combination with an experiment (or quasi-experiment).  There may be additional information that you can use to make judgments about what to keep and what to omit.

  Science involves judgment.  If you remove the judgment about individual weights by applying a mechanical rule, you push the judgment up a level to justifying the choice of rule.  Either way, these judgments will depend upon the context and content of your study.

Keith
------------------------
Keith A. Markus
John Jay College of Criminal Justice, CUNY
http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus
Frontiers of Test Validity Theory: Measurement, Causation and Meaning.
http://www.routledge.com/books/details/9781841692203/

messages.subject: Re: growth() model with two groups: equality constraints and 'group = '
messages.subject_clean: growth() model with two groups: equality constraints and 'group = '
messages.body_plain:
> The conclusion so far is that there is no difference between average slope. On the other hand, ModUn and ModHomog do not differ significantly

I'm confused by your use of "on the other hand," which suggests you might be testing constraints in the wrong order.  First, compare ModUn and ModHomog.  Because that test is not significant, you can't reject the null hypothesis that the effects of covariates on the latent slope do not differ across groups.  In other words, the effect of a covariate on the slope (i.e., the 2-way interaction between Time and the covariate) does not depend on Group (i.e., there is no evidence of a 3-way interaction between Group, Time, and a covariate).

Then, you can validly constrain the mean of the latent slope to test whether the effect of time differs across groups (i.e., is there a Time by Group 2-way interaction), controlling for those covariates.  Sounds like you can't reject the null on that one either.

> but ModHomog differs from the model that restricts both latent intercept and slope.

Please refer to parameters, not variables, as being constrained.  OK, so if you only constrain the latent slope's mean (I assume), the test is not significant.  But if you constrain the mean of both the latent intercept and the latent slope, then the test is significant?  That is a simultaneous of 2 different 2-way interactions.  You don't need to test those at the same time.  You tested the latent slope's mean and found not evidence of a group mean-difference above, so leave that constraint in place.

If you also want to test whether the mean of the latent intercept differs across groups (i.e., whether there is a significant "main" effect of Group on the outcome at Time 0), you first need to establish whether the effect of covariate(s) on the latent intercepts differs across groups (i.e., whether there is a covariate by Group 2-way interaction).  To do so, you can continue to use the model in which the latent slope's mean was constrained across groups (since you failed to reject that null hypothesis) as the baseline model (i.e., the new "unconstrained model" for the next test).  Compare that model to a model in which the effect of each covariate on the latent intercept is equal across groups (just like you did for effects on the latent slope).  If that constraint holds, you can then additionally constrain the mean of the latent intercept to equality across groups to see if fit gets worse (which would indicate a significant main effect of Group).

> However, when conducting follow-up test on the models with single restrictions on parameters one by one, no parameter-slope effect seems to differ between groups.

It is unclear which parameters you are talking about, so please be explicit.  Do you mean that you tested the effect of one covariate at a time of the latent intercept, and you didn't find a single significant group difference?  Even though the omnibus simultaneous test of all covariates' effects on the latent intercept was significant?  Well, I suppose many small differences could add up to a big enough discrepancy in the omnibus test.  But I think it is not easy to explain why this occurs because your covariates are probably correlated.  Therefore, their effects are also correlated, so constraining one covariate's effect at a time treats those tests (as though they are independent) doesn't tell you about the omnibus test with 100% certainty because those individual tests are correlated.  Correlated effects can lead to seemingly counter-intuitive results, like suppression effects, that are perfectly valid.

So I don't have specific advice about what to do.  If no individual covariate's effect shows strong evidence of differing across groups, then I suppose constraining them all across groups is justified even if that omnibus test is significant (maybe it's a Type I error?).  And maybe that means a subsequent test of equality of latent-intercept means would not be biased enough by the possibly invalid constraint to cause concern.  If you decide to report that test, I would recommend addressing that uncertainty as a limitation in your Discussion section.

> Does this then indicate the presence of a 3-way interaction?

No, it doesn't sound like it. See above for where to look for a 3-way interaction between Time, Group, and a covariate.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.subject: Pseudo R2 with multiple predictors
messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

I was asked to report pseudo-R2 values for two SEM models that have an observed binary outcome. lavaan provides a pseudo-R2 value that I believe is based on McKelvey & Zavoina (1975). If possible, I would like to provide bootstrap-based confidence intervals for the pseudo-R2 values. To do this, my plan is to calculate the pseudo-R2 estimate as a parameter in my lavaan model code and then use the boostrapLavaan() function to calculate confidence intervals. But I don't think that I am calculating the pseudo-R2 statistic properly when there are multiple predictor variables.

I used the formula provided in equation 15 of the Mplus Technical Appendixes <http://statmodel.com/download/techappen.pdf>: R2 = [pi^2 * V(x)] / [pi^2 * V(x) + V(delta)], where pi = regression coefficient associated with predictor variable x, and delta = the residual for the latent continuous response variable y* underlying the observed binary outcome y. I believe that Var(delta) = 1 when using probit regression.

Here is a reproducible example of what I would like to do. Borrowing code from Rosseel (2014) <http://www.personality-project.org/r/tutorials/summerschool.14/rosseel_sem_cat.pdf>, I created a binary version of the Holzinger & Swineford data (code in blue and output in red):

> library(lavaan)

> HS9 <- HolzingerSwineford1939[,c("x1","x2","x3","x4")]
> HSbinary <- as.data.frame( lapply(HS9, cut, 2, labels=FALSE) )

Here is the observed variance-covariance matrix for the data set.

> cov( HSbinary )
           x1           x2                x3                x4
x1 0.22790698 0.04255814 0.05806202 0.05333333
x2 0.04255814 0.25036545 0.06019934 0.05238095
x3 0.05806202 0.06019934 0.23526024 0.03523810
x4 0.05333333 0.05238095 0.03523810 0.24571429

When I treat x1 as binary outcome with a single binary predictor (x2), I can create a new parameter 'r2' that is the same as the lavaan pseudo-R2. Note, I had to provide the variance for the x2 predictor in the formula.

> model1 <- '
> x1 ~ g1*x2
> num := (g1^2)*0.2503654
> den := num + 1
> r2 := num/den
> '

> summary( fit1 <- lavaan( model1, estimator = 'wlsmv', data = HSbinary, ordered = 'x1' ), rsquare = T )

R-Square:
                   Estimate
    x1                0.051

Defined Parameters:
                   Estimate  Std.Err  z-value  P(>|z|)
    num               0.054    0.035    1.540    0.124
    den               1.054    0.035   30.227    0.000
    r2                0.051    0.031    1.623    0.105

However, when I have multiple predictors, my pseudo-R2 estimate is off (lavaan's pseudo-R2 = 0.127 and my version = 0.108). The equation provided in the Mplus Technical Appendixes is for a single predictor and I don't think my attempt to generalize this to the case of multiple predictors was successful. My guess is that this is because the predictors are correlated.

> model2 <- '
> x1 ~ g1*x2 + g2*x3
> num := (g1^2)*0.2503654 + (g2^2)*0.2352602
> den := num + 1
> r2 := num/den
> '

> summary( fit2 <- lavaan( model2, estimator = 'wlsmv', data = HSbinary, ordered = 'x1' ), rsquare = T )

R-Square:
                   Estimate
    x1                0.127

Defined Parameters:
                   Estimate  Std.Err  z-value  P(>|z|)
    num               0.121    0.050    2.414    0.016
    den               1.121    0.050   22.417    0.000
    r2                0.108    0.040    2.705    0.007

Is anyone able to help me reproduce lavaan's pseudo-R2 value in the case of multiple predictors?

Many thanks,

-Steve

messages.subject: Re: Setting equal differences between thresholds
messages.body_plain:
Karel,
If you do not have too many variables, this will work.  If you need more, then you will need to supply a longer list of parameter names in place of letters on line 4.

myThresholdFunction <- function(varNames, ...){
  nvar <- length(varNames)
  if(nvar > 13){warning('Not enough letters!')}
  thresholdNames <- matrix(letters[1:(nvar*2)], nrow=nvar, ncol=2, byrow=TRUE)
  thresholdText <- NULL
  constraintText <- NULL
  for(rep in 1:nvar){
    thresholdText <- rbind(thresholdText, paste0(varNames[rep], '|', thresholdNames[rep, 1], '*t1 + ', thresholdNames[rep, 2], '*t2'))
    if(rep > 1){constraintText <- rbind(constraintText, paste0(thresholdNames[rep-1,1], '-', thresholdNames[rep-1, 2], ' == ',
      thresholdNames[rep, 1], '-', thresholdNames[rep, 2]))}
  }
  thresholdString <- paste(thresholdText, collapse = '\n')
  cat(thresholdString)
  cat('\n')
  constraintString <- paste(constraintText, collapse = '\n')
  cat(constraintString)
}

myVarNames <- paste0('Item', 1:12)
myThresholdFunction(myVarNames)

KM

Hi!

I would like to validate an existing instrument for a particular sample. In the CFA, I obtained a measurement model with three factors (F1, F2, F3), with nice reliability for each factor and good fitting measures for the overall model. Does this negative value mean that something is wrong or that there is some frailty in the model?

In affirmative case, the simplest hypotheses to solve the problem are either to remove factor F3 (or F1), or to require F1 ~~ 0*F3. However, this imposition does not have theoretical mean.

What would you do in this case?

> > I wonder what to make of a SEM model that as a non-significant P-value for Chi-square under DWLS but a significant P-value under Robust.
>
> It's usually the other way around, since the robust correction is meant to correct for Type I error inflation (at least with continuous data, for which it was originally intended to be used).  But that is the average behavior over many samples.  You just have one sample, so you can't draw an inference about why this happened to happen.
>
> The uncorrected test statistic is only provided for the sake of completion (and because it is used in the robust chi-squared difference test).  You should pay attention only to the robust column because that is the one expected to behave better on average across many samples.  However, you have a very small sample, and past research has shown that even this robust test statistic has inflated error rates until sample sizes are very large, especially when categories are asymmetric.
>
> http://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/10705511.2014.859510
>
> > I tried also the Bayesian version. But there, I do not get a test-statistic for too many missing data
>
> Huh?  If you are looking for the chi-squared (derived from the minimum fit function using DWLS) in blavaan output, you won't find it with complete data because it is not a Bayesian statistic.  There is a PPP value, and some information criteria available for model comparison.
>
> > Can I use the Bayesian parameter estimates and use the test-statistics from the frequentist analysis? Or is the data quality such that I should not use the SEM at all?
>
> No, your test statistic is derived from the estimator, so you need to report one set of results or the other.  Again, you might be looking for something that isn't there in blavaan.  Perhaps this article will shed some light.
>

messages.subject_clean: lavaan WARNING: some observed variances are (at least) a factor 1000 times larger than others
messages.body_plain:
Τη Τετάρτη, 18 Οκτωβρίου 2017 - 9:10:53 π.μ. UTC+1, ο χρήστης Terrence Jorgensen έγραψε:
> > what this practically means for my model. Does this mean I should not trust this particular model because these unequal variances make it unreliable?
>
> The message is a warning because it might be a problem.  Estimators try to minimize the discrepancy between the observed and expected (i.e., model-implied) means and (co)variances.  If a variable has an observed variance == 1 and the model estimates imply it is only half as large, the discrepancy (residual) is only 1 - 0.5 = 0.5, but if a variable has an observed variance of 100, the same relative discrepancy (half as large: 50) is much larger in absolute magnitude (100-50=50).  So variables with much larger variances can dominate the estimation algorithm's search for the best-fitting parameter estimates, paying less attention to important discrepancies among variables with less variance.  Again, that is only a possibility, not a guarantee.
>
> > Presumably, the variances are so large due to the values of the variables so should I transform my variables in some way?
>
> Sure, you can divide the variable with large variance by 10 to express in larger units, so that the variance is 10^2 = 100 times smaller, making it closer in magnitude to other observed variances.  Assuming the estimator was not actually running into problems with the original data, you should get identical model fit, and your point and SE estimates involving the transformed variable should be the same except for a change in decimal place.
>
> > Could it also be a result of some of my variables not being normally distributed?
>
> No, nonnormal variables can also have either large or small variance.
>
> > I am not actually using the errors and I am using the Wald test to investigate the fit of the model and the predictors so how concerned should I be about non-normality in my case?
>
> Well, the Wald test for parameters also assumes normality of sampling distribution with the estimated SE, which assumes normal data.  Like with OLS regression, robustness to nonnormality is also a matter of degree, so it depends how must excess kurtosis the variables have.  To be conservative, you can use robust ML to adjust SEs and test statistics for nonnormality.  Some are available even with missing data when using FIML.
>
> fit <- sem(model, data, missing = "FIML", estimator = "MLR")
>
>
> Terrence D. Jorgensen
> Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
> Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
> UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen
>

Thanks so much Terrence!!!
I fitted the models the other day with transformed variables (divided by 10) and the fit and parameters were the same, meaning that the larger variances didn't really affect my model's fit. The final thing I would like to ask is whether in lavaan there is a way to check the regression assumptions: namely if I can produce plots of the residuals with the fitted values or with leverage points similar to those produced with the plot(model)  function when conducting normal multiple regression with lm.

Thanks
Thalia

totIndirect := indirect1+indirect2

totIndirect := a1*b1+a2*b2

messages.subject: Re: The different results in Lavaan and SmartPLS
messages.subject_clean: The different results in Lavaan and SmartPLS
messages.body_plain:
These packages apply completely different statistical methods. lavaan is a tool for factor-based SEM, while SmartPLS uses a composite-based procedure, partial leat squares path modeling. Differences between the methods are reason enough for a substantial difference in results. However, even if the two packages applied the very same statistical procedure, small differences in algorithms could still produce some differences in results.

library(semTools)
library(matrixpls)

## The industrialization and Political Democracy example

dem65 =~ y5 + y6 + y7 + y8

y6 ~~ y8

Hi,

A couple of comments to the example. (Disclaimer: I am the developer of of matrixpls)

> On 25 Oct 2017, at 5.58, Mauricio Garnier-Villarreal <mauga...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> As Edward explains, it is expected to see differences. But, we dont know how different from your example.
>
> But, for the an example, here is code that runs the same model and data with lavaan, and matrixpls, in general the PLS estimates are relatively close to the standardized parameters from lavaan, not the unstandardized

No, that does not hold generally.

What PLS does simply regression with scale scores formed as weighted sums of indicators. If you have indicators where the only source of measurement error is random noise, then the regression coefficients from regression with scale scores typically underestimates the regression paths. This underestimation is a function of reliabilities.

In this example, the results are close to one another because reliabilities are high.

> reliability(fit1)
           ind60     dem60     dem65     total
alpha  0.9023348 0.8587945 0.8827394 0.9149416
omega  0.9437375 0.8375193 0.8556193 0.9134989

>
> library(lavaan)
> library(semTools)
> library(matrixpls)
>
>
> ## The industrialization and Political Democracy example
> ## Bollen (1989), page 332. (Adopted from the lavaan package.)
> model <- '
> # latent variable definitions
> ind60 =~ x1 + x2 + x3
> dem60 =~ y1 + y2 + y3 + y4
> dem65 =~ y5 + y6 + y7 + y8
> # regressions
> dem60 ~ ind60
> dem65 ~ ind60 + dem60
> # residual correlations
> y1 ~~ y5
> y2 ~~ y4 + y6
> y3 ~~ y7
> y4 ~~ y8
> y6 ~~ y8
> '
>
> fit1 <- sem(model, data = PoliticalDemocracy, std.lv <http://std.lv>=T, meanstructure=T)
> summary(fit1, fit.measures=T, standardized=T, rsquare=T)
> reliability(fit1)
>
>
> political.out <- matrixpls(cov(PoliticalDemocracy),model, weightFun = weightFun.optim)

This code does not calculate the scale scores using PLS weights, but instead applies numerical optimization (by default BFGS) to maximize or minimize an optimization criterion. The default criterion is to maximize the R2 of the regression between the scale scores, but I have also implemented other criteria and it is easy to implement your own.

When the data are very reliable, then indicator weighting does not matter much. You can check this by comparing all the indicator weight systems implemented in matrixpls:

cbind(matrixpls(cov(PoliticalDemocracy),model, weightFun = weightFun.optim),
      matrixpls(cov(PoliticalDemocracy),model, weightFun = weightFun.fixed),
      matrixpls(cov(PoliticalDemocracy),model, weightFun = weightFun.pls),
      matrixpls(cov(PoliticalDemocracy),model, weightFun = weightFun.principal),
      matrixpls(cov(PoliticalDemocracy),model, weightFun = weightFun.factor))

They all produce nearly identical results.

                   [,1]      [,2]      [,3]      [,4]      [,5]
dem60~ind60  0.46193397 0.3931697 0.4027185 0.3962893 0.4252621
dem65~ind60  0.19440196 0.2004695 0.1960200 0.1964309 0.1710589
dem65~dem60  0.77472958 0.7823229 0.7858439 0.7844442 0.7860951

Note that PLS weights have important problems that you should be aware of. See for example here:

https://www.researchgate.net/publication/304253718_Partial_least_squares_path_modeling_Time_for_some_serious_second_thoughts

I am pretty sure that all the problems of PLS weights apply also if you optimize the weights to maximize R2, but I do not think that anyone has studied this.

Mikko

> The final thing I would like to ask is whether in lavaan there is a way to check the regression assumptions: namely if I can produce plots of the residuals with the fitted values or with leverage points similar to those produced with the plot(model)  function when conducting normal multiple regression with lm.

lavaan is a covariance-structure analysis program, so residuals in this context are the differences between observed and expected (model-implied) covariance matrices, not observed and expected (predicted) values per individual row of data.  You can use the estimated regression slopes to calculate predicted values manually (although you will only get them for rows with complete data on predictors), then calculate residuals manually (for rows without missing predictors).

messages.subject: Re: Handling plausible values in lavaan
messages.body_plain:
It sounds like you have 5 copies of the same data set, where each copy of the data set has different estimated factor scores (plausible values of the latent trait).

You could think of this as a missing data problem.  You have not observed the latent traits, and your IRT analysis has "imputed" them multiple (5) times.  You could therefore save the 5 data sets in a list, and pass them as data to the runMI() function in semTools, which will pool results by averaging parameter estimates across the 5 data sets, as well as pool the average SE per data set with the variability of estimates across 5 data sets.  I would expect this to yield nominal Type I error rates, although it would be less efficient than running a single latent regression model that includes the measurement model for the latent traits and the regression model among those latent traits (and any other variables in your model).

To do the missing-data trick, make sure you have the latest development versions of lavaan and semTools:

install.packages("lavaan", repos="http://www.da.ugent.be", type="source")
# install.packages("devtools") # if necessary, to install semTools below
devtools::install_github("simsem/semTools/semTools")

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.body_plain:
> How could I solve the problem?

The problem is either that (1) your model is not a good approximation to represent how your data are truly generated, or (2) your small sample of 186 means that a Heywood case is not terribly surprising.  You can test (1) by looking at your model's chi-squared fit statistic.  If it is significant, there is strong evidence your model is not an exact representation of the true data-generating process; you can consult other fitMeasures() to evaluate whether the model fits even approximately well.  You can test (2), i.e., whether sampling error is a plausible explanation, using the methods described here:

http://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1177/0049124112442138

If the model fits at least approximately well and you cannot rule out sampling error as the cause, then you could accept the solution as it is, and address the concern about the Heywood case by reporting the 95% CI, which must include plausible values (i.e., you can infer the true population correlation is within +/-1)

1) are the factor score estimates of the latent variables obtained as the mean and variance of the estimates of these in the Gibbs sampler after the chosen burn-in period; i.e. without being expressed in terms of the stuctural parameter estimates?

2) are there any studies comparing these Bayesian estimates of latent scores with those obtained in ML SEM via either the regression method or by minimising the sum of squares of the standardized residuals (I don't know which method is used in lavaan)?  What are the conclusions?

3) If I obtain new observations of the indicator variables, and want to then predict the latent scores associated with these new observations using blavaan, how can I do it?  This can be done in ML SEM because these are functions of the structural parameters, but I don't know how (if) this can be done in a Bayesian context.  This last point is particularly important to me because the latent scores are of primary importance and others need to use the measurement model to obtain their own latent scores given their data.

Thanks for any help.

messages.subject: Re: factor score estimates in blavaan (Bayesian lavaan)
messages.subject_clean: factor score estimates in blavaan (Bayesian lavaan)
messages.body_plain:
Bill

The later book by Song and Lee (2012) is more understandable in my opinion, and also the book by Kaplan (2014) has a couple of chapters about bayesian SEM. And I teach a 5 day course in Bayesian SEM (https://www.statscamp.org/summer-camp/advanced-sem) in case you are interested

1)  The factor scores are estimated as a parameter for each subject at each step of the gibbs sampler. The factor scores can be estimated through data augmentation, meaning that given the conditional model, and the scale constraints (for example setting the mean to-, and variance to 1), the factor scores can be estimated giving that this is enough information to constraint the data space for them. They are explicit in the SEM equation. blavaan doesnt export the factor scores by default, but you can ask it to

2) Not that I know of. A meaningful difference between de ML and Bayes factor scores, is that from ML you get 1 estimate of the factor scores, while in bayesian for each factor score for each subject you get a posterior distribution, from which you can use the mean of the posterior as the best single estimate, but you also have a measure of uncertainty for them.

3) If you get a new sample, you can run the model with blavaan and ask to export the factor scores with the jagextra argument, like this, asking to monitor "eta", eta is the name of the factors in the jags code that blavaan creates

fit51 <-  bcfa(mod51, data=dat, std.lv <http://std.lv>=T,
n.chains = 3, burnin=5000,
            sample=2000,
jagextra = list(monitor="eta"))

Also, for blavaan specific questions, it has its own google group, where the developer may see doubts faster
https://groups.google.com/forum/?fromgroups=#!forum/blavaan

bye

messages.subject: LISREL MIMIC model with no disturbance term
messages.subject_clean: LISREL MIMIC model with no disturbance term
messages.body_plain:
I am trying to reproduce the results in Fornell and Bookstein (1982) p.445-446 by using a different dataset. According to them, the MIMIC model can be estimated by both PLS and LISREL. More specifically, "if LISREL is specified in a MIMIC version with theta_epsilon symmetric (i.e. the errors of the y-variables are correlated), it will produce results identical to those from a two-construct PLS model with formative indicators". This should correspond to a MIMIC model with no disturbance term, i.e. a model where the latent variable is an exact linear combination of its causal indicators (see Hauser and Goldberger, 1971).

Lavaan estimates by default a disturbance term for every endogenous latent variable. If I want to remove it, is it sufficient to correlate the errors of the y-variables, like in the following example?

model <- '
  #formative indicators
  xi =~  y1 + y2 + y3 + y4
  #reflective indicators
  xi ~ x1 + x2 + x3
  #residual correlations
  y1 ~~ y2 + y3 + y4
  y2 ~~ y3 + y4
  y3 ~~ y4
'

Thanks a lot,

Simona

References:
Fornell C. and Bookstein F.L. (1982) Two Structural Equation Models: LISREL and PLS Applied to Consumer Exit-Voice Theory, Journal of Marketing Research, Vol. 19, No. 4, Special Issue on Causal Modeling, pp.440-452.
Hauser R.M. and Goldberger S. (1971) The Treatment of Unobservable Variables in Path Analysis, in Sociological Methodology, H.L. Costner, ed. San Francisco: Jossey-Bass, 81-117.

messages.body_plain:
I'm working with http://byrneslab.net/classes/lavaan_materials/Keeley_rawdata_select4.csv as a data file and generated the following:

keeley<-read.csv("../data/Keeley_rawdata_select4.csv")
keeley$coverSQ <- keeley$cover^2
keeley$group <- c(rep(1, nrow(keeley)/2), rep(0, nrow(keeley)/2))

compModel<-'

 coverEffect <~ cover + coverSQ

   rich ~ 1*coverEffect'

compFit <- sem(compModel, data=keeley,
               group = "group")

compFitConstrain <- sem(compModel, data=keeley,
               group = "group",
               group.equal=c("loadings", "intercepts", "means", "thresholds", "regressions", "residuals", "residual.covariances", "lv.variances", "lv.covariances"))

coef(compFitConstrain)

You'll note from the final coef that, despite throwing in all available options from group.equal, the loadings for the composite variables still differ.

> coef(compFitConstrain)
     coverEffect<~cover    coverEffect<~coverSQ                    .p4.
                 18.007                   3.290                 157.930
                   .p9.   coverEffect<~cover.g2 coverEffect<~coverSQ.g2
                 29.639                  67.594                 -39.960
                   .p4.                    .p9.
                157.930                  29.639

Is there an additional argument to group.equal that is not in the documentation? Note, this works if I constrain the coefficients to be equal in the model, but in my actual model I have 10 groups and many loadings, so would prefer to avoid such a model.

Note, this fit is with 0.6-1.1170, but the same issue is encountered on the version on CRAN.

messages.subject: Re: group.equal does not work with composite loadings?
messages.subject_clean: group.equal does not work with composite loadings?
messages.body_plain:
Jarrett,
Remember that composite loadings are not loadings as far as the matrix representation is concerned.  If you look at your summary output, you will see that they are parameterized as regressions (effect coefficients) -- or better yet extract the free parameters to see the matrices in which they reside.  As such, it is not clear that there is a simple way to write a groups.equal parameter that would anticipate which coefficients the user wanted to constrain and which to leave unconstrained.  From the interpreters perspective, a composite with 3 items and 1 predictor looks the same as a composite with 4 items.

One strategy would be to create the parameter table from the model syntax and then directly manipulate that.  Here is a simplified example with one composite and two groups.

require(lavaan)

myModel <- '
  compositeVar <~ x1 + x2 + x3
  x4 ~ c(d,d)*compositeVar
  x5 ~ compositeVar
  x6 ~ compositeVar
  x4~~x4
  x5~~x5
  x6~~x6

  d == .5
  '

myTable <- lavaanify(myModel, ngroups=2)
myTable

pickMeForA <- myTable$lhs == 'compositeVar' & myTable$rhs == 'x1'
pickMeForB <- myTable$lhs == 'compositeVar' & myTable$rhs == 'x2'
pickMeForC <- myTable$lhs == 'compositeVar' & myTable$rhs == 'x3'

myTable$label[pickMeForA] <- 'a'
myTable$label[pickMeForB] <- 'b'
myTable$label[pickMeForC] <- 'c'
myTable

myFit <- lavaan(myTable, data=HolzingerSwineford1939, group='sex')
summary(myFit)

Keith

Keith A. Markus

http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus
Frontiers of Test Validity Theory: Measurement, Causation and Meaning.
http://www.routledge.com/books/details/9781841692203/

messages.body_plain:
Jarrett,
  My bad, I let that reply go a little too soon.  Try this instead.  One the model is in table form, it is not enough to give two parameters the same label.  You need to add the constraint as a line of the parameter table.

require(lavaan)

myModel <- '
  compositeVar <~ x1 + x2 + x3
  x4 ~ c(d,d)*compositeVar
  x5 ~ compositeVar
  x6 ~ compositeVar
  x4~~x4
  x5~~x5
  x6~~x6

  d == .5
  '

myTable <- lavaanify(myModel, ngroups=2)
myTable

pickMeForA <- myTable$lhs == 'compositeVar' & myTable$rhs == 'x1'
pickMeForB <- myTable$lhs == 'compositeVar' & myTable$rhs == 'x2'
pickMeForC <- myTable$lhs == 'compositeVar' & myTable$rhs == 'x3'

myTable$label[pickMeForA] <- 'a'
myTable$label[pickMeForB] <- 'b'
myTable$label[pickMeForC] <- 'c'
myTable

for(choice in list(pickMeForA, pickMeForB, pickMeForC)){
  collectLabels <- myTable$plabel[choice]
  lastLine <- max(myTable$id)
  for(iter in 2:length(collectLabels)){
    newLine <- data.frame(
      id = lastLine + iter,
      lhs = collectLabels[iter-1],
      op = '==',
      rhs = collectLabels[iter],
      user = NA,
      block = 0,
      group = 0,
      free = 0,
      ustart = NA,
      exo = 0,
      label = '',
      plabel = '')
    myTable <- rbind(myTable, newLine)

  }
}
myTable

myFit <- lavaan(myTable, data=HolzingerSwineford1939, group='sex')
summary(myFit)

Keith

> Pawel,
> Perhaps the source of the confusion here involves the scope of DWLS.  Today, DWLS is perhaps most commonly used in conjunction with threshold models for ordinal data.  However, it was developed independently and, I believe, earlier.  If I am not mistaken, DWLS was introduced into LISREL as a computationally less demanding alternative to WLS (ADF).  Both were presented as methods for modeling non-normal continuous data.  In this respect, DWLS differs from mean-adjusted and mean-and-variance-adjusted WLS which I believe were both developed specifically in the context of threshold models for categorical data.
>
> So, when you choose DWLS in Lavaan, you are not automatically choosing to use threshold models.  You are simply choosing an estimation technique for the model that you specified.  You can confirm this by looking at the parameters listed in the summary output or parameter matrices. If you use DWLS to estimate a continuous variable model, you will not see thresholds among the parameters.
>
> # The Holzinger and Swineford (1939) example
> HS.model <- ' visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3
>               textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
>               speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9 '
>
> fit <- lavaan(HS.model, data=HolzingerSwineford1939,
>               auto.var=TRUE, auto.fix.first=TRUE,
>               auto.cov.lv.x=TRUE, estimator='DWLS')
>
> summary(fit)
> lavInspect(object=fit, what='free')

messages.subject_clean: How to implement a try catch in lavaan error
messages.body_plain:
Ellas,
Note that seq(1000, 2000, by=1000) is the same as c(1000, 2000).

Also, note that supplying a sample.cov and changing the sample.nobs does not recompute the sample.cov based on sample.nobs.

require(lavaan)

myModel <- '
  Factor =~ x1 + x2 + x3
  Factor ~~ 1*Factor
  x1 ~~ x1
  x2 ~~ x2
  x3 ~~ x3
  '

myOutput <- list()         # Initiallize empty list to collect output
for(data.size in seq(200,350,by=50)){   # Note: data set has only 301 cases
  tryCatch({
    data.cov <- cov(HolzingerSwineford1939[1:data.size,7:9])
    myFit <- sem(myModel, sample.cov=data.cov, sample.nobs=data.size)
    myOutput <- append(myOutput, myFit)
  })
}
myOutput  # Output contains fit for 200, 250, and 300 but not 350, which produced an error

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am struggling with my data analysis and I would really appreciate insight into where I am going wrong.

I administered a 51 item Attitude questionnaire to 481 students.

Attitude is the overarching latent variable/construct.

I have clustered the 51 items into 13 Themes (latent variables/constructs).

These Themes are weakly to moderately correlated (0.3 to 0.6)

These 13 Themes can be further clustered into 4 higher order latent variables.

#4 higher order latent variables

I have tried FIRST coding SELF_PROF <-  ITEM6+ITEM17+ITEM22+ITEM32+ITEM41 then putting these 4 higher orders into the SEM model – no luck – model won’t fit.

I have tried creating new variables in my dataset: SELF_PROF, SS_TYPE etc. with the sum of these items – no luck – model won’t fit.

I have 4 Dependent/Predictor variables:

ENG_PROF, ENG_COUNTRY, AGE, MTHS_THRU_ENG, SS_TYPE, EMI_REQ

ATT_DATA ~ GEN*AGE

ATT_DATA ~ GEN*ENG_COUNTRY

ATT_DATA ~ AGE*ACAD_SUBJ

ATT_DATA ~ AGE*ENG_PROF

ATT_DATA ~ AGE*MTHS_THRU_ENG

ATT_DATA ~ AREA*UNI_TYPE

ATT_DATA ~ AREA*ENG_PROF

ATT_DATA ~ AREA*SS_TYPE

ATT_DATA ~ AREA*EMI_REQ

ATT_DATA ~ ENG_PROF*MTHS_THRU_ENG

ATT_DATA ~ ENG_PROF*ENG_COUNTRY

ATT_DATA ~ EMI_REQ*ENG_COUNTRY

As you can see I have MANY variables – and I think this is the root cause of my problem – no model is being fit.

Is there another way of coding that I am missing?

I also don't see how I can 'break the model up' and run separate models so that Lavaan can handle it.

Any help would be very much greatly appreciated.

messages.subject: Re: Too many variables
messages.body_plain:
Samantha,

This is a very broad question not specific to Lavaan.  It might be better suited for SEMNET.

Bear in mind that clustering items based on similarity does not guarantee that they will fit a linear common factor model.  It is just a hypothesis.  Failure is an option.

I would suggest the following:

Do not compute sum scores in your data set.  Stick to latent variable modeling using only the item scores.

Fit the one-factor model for each first level factor using only the items for that factor.  For factors with more than 3 items, evaluate the fit and parameter estimates.  For factors with 3 items, evaluate the parameter estimates.

Combine just the factors that look plausible based on their one-factor models into a single level CFA with correlated factors.  Evaluate fit and parameter estimates to look for problems.

Fit a series of models with a single 2nd order factor using just the items and first-order factors that correspond to that 2nd order factor.  Assess fit and parameter estimates.

Combine only the models for 2nd order factors that look plausible based on the prior analyses into your full model with multiple 2nd order factors.

This procedure is as much exploratory as confirmatory.  So, report the multi-step procedure fully and accurately with your results.

Keith
------------------------
Keith A. Markus
John Jay College of Criminal Justice, CUNY
http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus
Frontiers of Test Validity Theory: Measurement, Causation and Meaning.
http://www.routledge.com/books/details/9781841692203/

> > > Do not compute sum scores in your data set.  Stick to latent variable modeling using only the item scores.
> > >
> > > Fit the one-factor model for each first level factor using only the items for that factor.  For factors with more than 3 items, evaluate the fit and parameter estimates.  For factors with 3 items, evaluate the parameter estimates.
> > >
> > > Combine just the factors that look plausible based on their one-factor models into a single level CFA with correlated factors.  Evaluate fit and parameter estimates to look for problems.
> > >
> > > Fit a series of models with a single 2nd order factor using just the items and first-order factors that correspond to that 2nd order factor.  Assess fit and parameter estimates.
> > >
> > > Combine only the models for 2nd order factors that look plausible based on the prior analyses into your full model with multiple 2nd order factors.
> > >
> > > This procedure is as much exploratory as confirmatory.  So, report the multi-step procedure fully and accurately with your results.

messages.body_plain:
Why are you doing this?  Not only is it a problem to fit a model to a correlation matrix instead of a covariance matrix:

http://www.statpower.net/Content/319SEM/Reading/Cudeck89.pdf

But if you estimate polychoric correlations first, then fit a model to those correlations, your results will be biased because you will not have taken into account the uncertainty about the estimated correlations.  It would be even more dishonest to change correlations to exactly zero just because they are close to zero, because then you don't even have estimates anymore, nor the estimated uncertainty necessary to account for in Step 2.  Instead, just fit your model to your raw data, specifying which variables should be treated as ordinal:

http://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/cat.html

lavaan will estimate the polychoric correlations automatically and take their uncertainty into account.

Note that robust ML estimation may provide unbiased estimates with 5-7 categories, depending how asymmetric the thresholds are.

http://psych.colorado.edu/~willcutt/pdfs/Rhemtulla_2012.pdf

Terrence D. Jorgensen

Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

messages.subject: Re: Dealing with measurement invariance in an intervention study
messages.subject_clean: Dealing with measurement invariance in an intervention study
messages.body_plain:
> For this 2x2 design I want to assess measurement invariance.

2 (random Likert scale) x 2 (random learning environment) x 2 (time points) pretest-posttest design.  So you have 4 groups and 2 occasions.  How do the scales differ?  Are the 2 scales supposed to be parallel forms?  That is, does it make sense to constrain loadings/intercepts from one scale to be equal to loadings/intercepts from the other scale?

> Do I need to constrain the intercepts for the groups and both measurement points?

Yes, in order to compare latent means (right? you didn't specify) across all 8 contexts, it is necessary that the measurement parameters (loadings AND intercepts) are constrained across those contexts.  Given the experimental design (random assignment to 4 groups), I think you can start with a model that already imposes equality constraints at Time 1 because there is no reason to suspect those are different populations.  You can then further constrain the Time-2 measurement parameters to equal Time 1.  You could still test invariance by beginning with an unconstrained Time-1 measurement model, but it would be a less parsimonious baseline model to start with.

> Recht_A_1 ~ c(T1, T1, T1, T1)*1
> Recht_A_2 ~ c(T2, T2, T2, T2)*1
> ...
>
> Recht_B_1 ~ c(T1, T1, T1, T1)*1
> Recht_B_2 ~ c(T2, T2, T2, T2)*1
> ...

You need to specify a vector of labels to constrain parameters across groups (as I edited above).  Providing 1 label will only apply that label  to the first group.

http://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/groups.html

> I'm not only interested in mean differences, but as well in the influence of covariate and outcomes (reading ability, learning disability or socio economic status).

That complicates things if you try to do everything in one model.  I would first try establishing invariance of the factor model with respect to your experimental groups and time.  If (at least partial) invariance holds, add covariate(s) predicting the factor to see if the model still fits well.  If not, then you may need to allow the covariate to directly affect at least one indicator as well as the factor, implying lack of measurement invariance with respect to that covariate (look up literature about MIMIC or Restricted Factor Analysis models for testing measurement invariance).  If you can establish (at least partial) invariance with respect to the covariate(s) as well, then add the outcome variable(s) as a predictive validity check.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen
